name: Audit & Tax Professional
description: CPA and audit knowledge: financial statements, GAAP/IFRS, IRC sections, Excel audit patterns, variance analysis, internal controls.

nodes.content: variance analysis: the process of identifying the difference between planned (budgeted) and actual financial figures; root causes include timing differences, allocation errors, data entry mistakes, and excluded rows in Excel SUM formulas

Excel audit gotcha — inserted row outside SUM range: when a row is inserted between the last row of a SUM range and the SUM formula cell, Excel does NOT automatically expand the range; the new row's values are excluded from the total, creating a variance equal to the sum of all excluded rows

Excel formula errors in financial workbooks: #REF! indicates a deleted or moved cell reference; #VALUE! indicates wrong data type in formula; #DIV/0! indicates division by zero (often from blank denominators in ratio calculations); all require manual investigation before relying on adjacent totals

GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles): the standard framework for financial accounting in the United States, governed by FASB; key principles include revenue recognition (ASC 606), lease accounting (ASC 842), and fair value measurement (ASC 820)

revenue recognition under ASC 606: five-step model — (1) identify the contract, (2) identify performance obligations, (3) determine transaction price, (4) allocate price to obligations, (5) recognize revenue when/as obligations satisfied; common audit risk: premature recognition before delivery

lease accounting under ASC 842: operating leases now appear on the balance sheet as right-of-use (ROU) assets and lease liabilities; audit focus: completeness of lease inventory, discount rate used, lease term classification, short-term lease practical expedient

internal controls: policies and procedures that safeguard assets and ensure reliability of financial reporting; COSO framework defines five components — control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information & communication, monitoring; SOX Section 404 requires management and auditor assessment of internal controls for public companies

audit materiality: the threshold above which misstatements could influence user decisions; typically calculated as a percentage of a benchmark (e.g., 5% of pre-tax income, 0.5% of total assets, 1% of revenue); performance materiality is set lower (often 50–75% of overall materiality) to provide a buffer

IRC Section 179: allows businesses to deduct the full cost of qualifying equipment and software in the year placed in service rather than depreciating over multiple years; 2024 limit is $1,220,000; phases out dollar-for-dollar when property placed in service exceeds $3,050,000

depreciation methods for tax vs. book: MACRS (Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System) is required for federal tax; straight-line, declining balance, and units-of-production are common for book (GAAP); the difference creates deferred tax assets or liabilities on the balance sheet

accrual accounting vs. cash basis: GAAP requires accrual — revenue recognized when earned, expenses when incurred, regardless of cash flow; cash basis records transactions only when cash changes hands; most small businesses use cash basis for tax (IRC §446); audit focus on accruals at period-end

accounts receivable aging: categorizes outstanding receivables by how long they have been unpaid (0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+ days); audit procedures include confirmation letters to debtors, testing subsequent cash collections, and evaluating adequacy of the allowance for doubtful accounts

journal entry testing: high-risk audit area; auditors look for manual JEs posted by unusual users, at unusual times (late night, weekends), with round numbers, or to unusual accounts; Benford's Law analysis flags anomalies in leading digits of large transaction populations

IFRS vs. GAAP key differences: IFRS allows revaluation of PP&E to fair value; GAAP uses historical cost; IFRS prohibits LIFO inventory method; GAAP permits LIFO; IFRS uses single-step impairment test; GAAP uses two-step; IFRS financial statements prepared on going concern basis unless management intends to liquidate

trial balance reconciliation: the process of ensuring debits equal credits after all entries; common reconciling items include unrecorded accruals, intercompany eliminations, timing differences between subsidiary ledgers and the general ledger, and bank reconciliation items (outstanding checks, deposits in transit)

goodwill impairment testing under ASC 350: goodwill is no longer amortized under GAAP (private companies may elect to amortize over 10 years); annual impairment test compares fair value of reporting unit to its carrying amount; qualitative assessment ('step zero') may bypass quantitative test if impairment is unlikely
